clinicalPearls: Internal impingement describes contact between the articular (undersurface) fibres of the posterosuperior rotator cuff and the posterosuperior glenoid labrum when the arm is abducted and maximally externally rotated.
It characteristically affects overhead athletes such as throwers, tennis players and swimmers, who present with posterior shoulder pain in the late cocking phase.

Although a degree of posterosuperior contact is physiological in abduction and external rotation, it becomes pathological when repetitive, causing articular-sided cuff fraying and posterosuperior labral damage.
Glenohumeral internal rotation deficit from posteroinferior capsular tightness is a central contributing factor and a key rehabilitation target.
Scapular dyskinesis and subtle anterior microinstability shift the contact zone and aggravate the impingement, so assess the whole kinetic chain.
It is distinct from classic external subacromial impingement; the pain is posterior and provoked in the abducted externally rotated position rather than on forward elevation.
First-line management is non-operative, emphasising posterior capsular stretching, scapular control and correction of throwing mechanics.

Surgery is reserved for refractory cases and addresses the specific pathology found, such as debridement of articular-sided cuff fraying and labral treatment, rather than routine subacromial decompression.
reference.pathophysiology: During the late cocking phase of overhead activity the abducted, maximally externally rotated humerus brings the articular surface of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus into contact with the posterosuperior glenoid rim and labrum. When repetitive, this normally protective contact produces shear and compressive loading that frays the undersurface of the cuff and damages the posterosuperior labrum. A tight posteroinferior capsule causes glenohumeral internal rotation deficit and a posterosuperior shift of the humeral rotation point, increasing the peel-back force on the biceps-labral complex and the degree of contact. Concurrent anterior capsular laxity or microinstability and scapular malposition further increase external rotation and posterior contact. The result is a self-perpetuating cycle of articular-sided partial cuff tearing, labral injury and pain that limits throwing performance.
additionalDifferentials: Articular-sided partial rotator cuff tear from other causes
additionalInvestigations: MR arthrography to demonstrate articular-sided cuff fraying and posterosuperior labral pathology
Standard MRI to assess cuff, labrum and any cysts
Assessment and quantification of glenohumeral internal rotation deficit
Evaluation of scapular kinematics and posture
Examination for anterior microinstability including apprehension and relocation testing
Diagnostic arthroscopy with dynamic assessment in abduction and external rotation for refractory cases
redFlags: Progressive weakness suggesting a significant or full-thickness rotator cuff tear
Features of frank instability with recurrent subluxation
Infraspinatus wasting suggesting suprascapular nerve involvement or a paralabral cyst
Night and rest pain unrelated to activity raising concern for other pathology
reference.prognosis: Most overhead athletes improve with a structured programme addressing posterior capsular tightness, scapular control and throwing mechanics, though return to the pre-injury level of high-demand throwing is not guaranteed. Refractory structural lesions may require arthroscopic treatment, with variable rates of return to elite performance.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as external subacromial impingement and performing an inappropriate acromioplasty.
Neglecting glenohumeral internal rotation deficit and scapular dyskinesis, the principal reversible drivers.
Interpreting the physiological posterosuperior contact seen on imaging as pathological in an asymptomatic athlete.
Overlooking associated anterior microinstability that perpetuates the impingement.
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma
